summary: Specifies the forwarding behavior that lets Segment Routing run over the MPLS data plane. A packet is steered through a chosen list of instructions called segments, which are carried as a stack of MPLS labels, so the path is set at the source instead of by per-flow state in the network.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8660 defines how Segment Routing uses Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) labels to forward packets. A packet carries a label stack that directs routers through the chosen segments without changing the MPLS forwarding plane.

questions: how does segment routing use mpls labels
what is an srgb in segment routing
subtitle: How Segment Routing rides on ordinary MPLS: segments are labels, the route is a stack of them, and the forwarding plane stays unchanged.

tldr.problem: Segment Routing steers a packet through a list of instructions called segments, but operators already run MPLS forwarding hardware and need to know exactly how segments map onto it.
tldr.mechanism: Each segment ID (SID) is an MPLS label, or an index turned into a label inside a router's Segment Routing Global Block (SRGB). The list of segments is a stack of MPLS labels, and routers apply the PUSH, CONTINUE and NEXT operations to it.
tldr.outcome: Segment Routing runs over MPLS with no change to the forwarding plane. The RFC also defines how to resolve two segments that map to the same incoming label, and leaves the control plane to other documents.

sections.title: What This Document Covers
sections.content:
The Segment Routing architecture (RFC 8402) can be applied to the MPLS architecture with no change to the MPLS forwarding plane. This RFC specifies the forwarding-plane behavior for that case, called SR-MPLS.

It deliberately does not cover the control plane. Protocols such as OSPF (RFC 8665), OSPFv3 (RFC 8666) and IS-IS (RFC 8667) carry segment information. Coexistence of SR with LDP is in RFC 8661.

The RFC calls any entity that installs forwarding entries into the MPLS data plane an MPLS Control Plane Client (MCC). Local configuration and policy are examples of MCCs.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC defines the packet-forwarding rules for Segment Routing over MPLS. Other documents define how routers learn or choose the segments.

sections.title: Segments as Labels and Label Blocks
sections.content:
In SR-MPLS a SID is represented by an MPLS label or by an index. A global SID is a label, or an index that maps to a label inside the router's Segment Routing Global Block (SRGB). A local SID may come from the Segment Routing Local Block (SRLB) or from any unused label that is not a special-purpose label.

The MCC MUST make sure each label used for a SID is unique on the router, meaning it represents only that SID and nothing else, and MUST NOT come from the special-purpose label range (RFC 7274). Labels are per-platform downstream allocated labels.

The SRGB need not be one contiguous range. It is a list of non-overlapping label ranges, none of which may overlap reserved labels. If a node's SRGB breaks these rules, every router in the routing domain MUST ignore it and treat the node as having no SRGB. The SRGB may only be used for global SIDs.

An operator may give the same prefix several SIDs, each with a different forwarding behavior, such as a different path or different ECMP behavior. Operators SHOULD configure at least one node segment per routing instance, topology or algorithm so that the node is reachable.
sections.plainLanguage: A segment is represented by an MPLS label or by an index that maps to a label. Each router must keep its labels unique, and its global label ranges must follow the rules in the RFC.

sections.title: Turning an Index into a Label
sections.content:
A control protocol such as IS-IS or OSPF supplies a SID index I. The MCC turns it into a label using the SRGB of the router that will receive the packet. The SRGB size is the sum of the sizes of all its ranges, and the index must satisfy 0 =< I < size, otherwise no label can be calculated.

The label is found by walking the ranges in order, skipping whole ranges while the index is larger than their size, then adding the remainder to the low end of the range where the index falls. With a single range this is simply the start of the range plus the index.

Because each neighbor may have its own SRGB, the sender uses the receiving neighbor's SRGB to compute the outgoing label. When a prefix is redistributed between routing protocol instances, the index is passed along only if both instances have the same SRGB. Otherwise the receiving instance allocates a fresh index relative to its own SRGB.
sections.plainLanguage: A router converts a segment index into a label using the receiving router’s Segment Routing Global Block. If the index falls outside that block, the router cannot calculate a label for it.

sections.title: When Two Segments Want the Same Label
sections.content:
Because of an error or misconfiguration, different FECs (forwarding equivalence classes, here things like a prefix, an adjacency, an SR Policy or a Mirror SID) can map to the same incoming label. An implementation MUST NOT let the MCCs on one router assign the same incoming label to more than one SR FEC. When a collision does occur, the RFC gives a recommended procedure that must be deterministic: the same FEC must win regardless of the order in which the advertisements arrive, so first-come, first-served is not allowed.

The default tiebreaking rules SHOULD be implemented:

  • Keep only the FECs with the lowest administrative distance (an 8-bit value, lower is better). An explicit, static SID assignment outside the SRGB beats a dynamic one, and a Binding SID for an SR Policy always has a worse default distance than other FEC types.
  • If more than one remains, pick the smallest numerical FEC value, comparing FEC type, then address family, then the encoded fields.

Losing FECs are handled as if they had no label. Operators MUST deploy routers using the same tiebreaking rules within an IGP flooding area. A FEC that loses its incoming label MUST NOT be installed with an outgoing SR label based on the SID of the lost label.
sections.plainLanguage: Two forwarding classes must not claim the same incoming label on one router. If a collision occurs, routers use deterministic tie-breaking so the same class wins regardless of arrival order.

sections.title: PUSH, CONTINUE and NEXT
sections.content:
The three operations defined in RFC 8402 map directly onto standard MPLS actions:

  • PUSH puts one or more labels on top of an incoming packet and sends it out of an interface, which may be physical or virtual (for example a UDP tunnel or an L2TPv3 tunnel). Setting the TTL and Traffic Class fields is left to local policy.
  • CONTINUE swaps the incoming label for an outgoing label.
  • NEXT pops the topmost label. What happens next depends on the instruction attached to the popped SID. For an Adj-SID, the packet is sent out the matching interface to the neighbor.

A Mirror SID is a special case: the router pops the label and then looks up the exposed packet in a mirrored forwarding table. The packet underneath may or may not be an MPLS packet.

The active segment of a packet is simply its topmost label.
sections.plainLanguage: The forwarding plane has three segment operations: PUSH adds labels, CONTINUE swaps the top label, and NEXT removes it. The router then follows the instruction attached to the active segment.

sections.title: Forwarding Rules for Global and Local SIDs
sections.content:
For a global SID, when a router applies PUSH or CONTINUE toward neighbor N, it first checks the neighbor. If N does not support SR, or advertises an invalid or too-small SRGB, the router forwards using standard MPLS if possible, else uses another next hop, else drops the packet.

Otherwise it calculates the outgoing label with the SRGB of N. For PUSH it pushes that label, and for CONTINUE it swaps the incoming label for it. For NEXT it pops the top label and applies the instruction of the popped label.

Local SIDs behave more simply. A local SID is just an MPLS label, so PUSH is an ordinary label push and CONTINUE is an ordinary label swap, with the outgoing label chosen by the MCC on the router. NEXT is the same as for global SIDs. The RFC covers the outgoing label only for the top label; stacks that encode a full policy or traffic-engineering tunnel are left to other documents.
sections.plainLanguage: For a global segment, the sender calculates the outgoing label from the next router’s label block. If that router cannot use Segment Routing, the sender tries ordinary MPLS, another next hop, or drops the packet.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
The appendix walks through a network where the operator defines an SRGB of [1000,5000] and gives the loopback of router R8 the global index 8. R1 wants to send an IPv4 packet to R8. The next hop, R2, has the SRGB [1000,5000], so R1 pushes the label 1008.

R2 is not the penultimate hop, so it applies CONTINUE and sends the packet to R3 with label 1008, using one of the two links between them (ECMP). R3 is the penultimate hop, so it performs penultimate hop popping, which is a NEXT operation, and sends a plain IPv4 packet to R8.

The appendix also gives fourteen worked examples of label collision resolution and two on how a collision affects the outgoing label.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC’s example shows a router adding the label for a destination, middle routers forwarding it, and the penultimate router removing it. The final router receives the original IP packet.

sections.title: Manageability and Security
sections.content:
The RFC says Segment Routing introduces no change to the MPLS data plane, so the manageability considerations of RFC 8402 apply. Operations, Administration and Maintenance use cases and procedures for the MPLS data plane are in RFC 8403 and RFC 8287.

Security is handled in one sentence: the document introduces no additional security requirements or mechanisms beyond those in RFC 8402. It has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC does not add security mechanisms or requirements to Segment Routing. It relies on the security guidance in the Segment Routing architecture.
